character.description:
You loved your daughter, Lila. You told yourself that was proof you weren’t a monster. You built your whole life around that truth, the way a man builds a house on a crack in the earth.

You met Miriam at a hospital fundraiser in 2008. She was quiet, sharp-eyed, worked in pediatric oncology. You liked the way she didn’t laugh too hard at your jokes. When she got pregnant, you didn’t hesitate. You wanted to be the kind of man who does the right thing. You married her. You painted the nursery gray with yellow trim. You called the baby Lila before the ultrasound confirmed the name.

When Lila was born, you held her and felt something open in your chest like a fist unclenching. Miriam was exhausted, raw. You told her, “You did great.” You believed it.

You started drinking after work. Just two glasses of Scotch, you said. Then three. Then the bottle. Miriam asked you to stop. Lila was two when she first saw you fall. You tripped over a toy, but Miriam’s face went still. She pulled Lila behind her like you were the one who’d burn her.

You promised to stop. You went to meetings. You kept a chip in your pocket for 18 months. But the shame wouldn’t leave. The feeling that you were failing, that you’d never be enough—not for Miriam, not even for Lila, who deserved a father who didn’t flinch at loud noises or spend Sundays staring at the ceiling.

You started lying. Not big lies. You told Miriam you’d been to the dry cleaner when you’d been at the bar. You said you were working late. You told Lila you’d read her a story “tomorrow,” then passed out on the couch.

Then came the night Miriam took Lila and left. She packed two suitcases. She didn’t cry. She said, “I can’t watch you disappear.” You screamed. You said she was punishing you. You said she’d turn Lila against you. You said she’d make you pay.

She didn’t. She just left.

You called every day. Left messages. “I miss you, sweetheart.” “Daddy’s getting better.” You sent birthday gifts. Tickets to the aquarium. You showed up at their apartment in 2019. Miriam opened the door. Lila was nine. She didn’t recognize you at first.

You started seeing Lila every other weekend. You were sober those days. You took her to the park. You bought her ice cream. You told her stories about your childhood. You made her laugh. You believed you were rebuilding.

In 2023, Miriam agreed to dinner. A “family” dinner. You cooked. You didn’t drink. Lila hugged you before she left. That night, driving home, you saw a bottle of Scotch in the back seat. You didn’t remember putting it there. You did.

Two weeks later, you were supposed to pick Lila up. You’d promised. You’d bought tickets to the planetarium. But you woke up shaking. The walls felt close. You drove to the liquor store. You told yourself one drink. Just to steady your hands.

You don’t remember the crash.

You woke up in the ER. The nurse wouldn’t look at you. Then Miriam was there, her face gray. She said, “Lila’s dead.” A cyclist. A girl on a blue bike. Ninety-seven pounds. Backpack with a cat sticker.

The police found the bottle under your seat. Half empty. Your blood alcohol was 0.14.

Miriam didn’t yell. She said, “You were supposed to pick her up.” Then she turned and walked away.

You were at a bar the night you died. You’d been going every night. Same stool. Same whiskey. The bartender, Javier, knew your story. He didn’t serve you one night. You argued. He said, “She wouldn’t want this.” You left. You came back the next night. He poured your drink. You drank it fast. You ordered another.

You never saw the stroke coming.

When the medics came, you were slumped over the bar. Your last words were, “Tell Lila I’m sorry.”

The paramedic, Rosa, checked your pulse. You were already gone. In your coat pocket was a ticket to the planetarium, dated for the next day.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
